ru: собираюсь, буду (сокращение от going to — только о будущем)
type: informal — a spoken reduction, written only in dialogue, texts and lyrics
register: informal — universal in American speech, out of place in anything edited
question: *You gonna eat that?* — in a casual question the *are* vanishes along with the reduction; the full form is *Are you going to eat that?*
contrast: *Gonna* is only the future *going to*. When *going to* means literal movement it never reduces: *I'm going to the store* stays as it is, and ✗ *I'm gonna the store* is not English. The test is simple — a verb has to follow (*gonna leave*, *gonna rain*, *gonna be fine*), never a noun or a place. Compare *wanna*, which has the mirror-image rule.

senses.gloss: The reduced *going to* of the future.
examples: I'm *gonna* call her back in a minute.
It's *gonna* rain before we get home.
What are you *gonna* do about it?

ru: хочу, хочешь (сокращение от want to)
type: informal — a spoken reduction, written only in dialogue, texts and lyrics
register: informal — heard in nearly every conversation, never used in edited prose
question: *Wanna grab lunch?* — the whole *Do you* is dropped, which is the ordinary American way of proposing something.
contrast: *Wanna* is *want to* and nothing else, so a verb has to follow: *I wanna go*, but ✗ *I wanna a coffee*. In speech *I want a coffee* reduces to almost the same sound, yet it is written *want a* — the noun version has no *wanna* spelling. There is a second, subtler block: when a subject stands between the two words, the reduction is impossible. *Who do you want to win?* cannot become ✗ *Who do you wanna win?*, because *who* is the subject of *win*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *want to* before a verb.
examples: I *wanna* leave before the traffic starts.
Do you *wanna* come with us?
She doesn't *wanna* talk about it yet.

ru: надо, должен; а также «есть у меня» (от have got to и have got a)
type: informal — a spoken reduction of the two uses of *have got*
register: informal — normal in speech, written only in dialogue and texts
ambiguity: Two different sentences reduce to the same *gotta*. Before a verb it is *got to* and means obligation: *I gotta go* is *I have got to go*. Before a noun the final *-a* is itself the article *a*: *I gotta minute* is *I have got a minute*. That is why ✗ *I gotta a minute?* is wrong — it writes the article twice.
question: *Gotta minute?* — the *Have you* is dropped completely. The full form is *Have you got a minute?*
contrast: *Gotta* reduces *have got*, never the past tense *got*: *I got a letter yesterday* has nothing to do with it. Americans usually drop the *have* as well (*I gotta go*, rarely *I've gotta go*), which is fine in speech; in writing use *have to* or *have got to*. Compare *hafta*, which carries the same obligation through *have to*.

senses.gloss: Obligation — the reduced *have got to*.
examples: I *gotta* go — my bus leaves in five minutes.
You *gotta* see the new place, it's enormous.
We *gotta* be at the airport by six.

senses.gloss: Possession — the reduced *have got a*, with the article already inside it.
examples: I *gotta* friend who does exactly this kind of work.
You *gotta* minute? I need to ask you something.
He's *gotta* new job downtown.

ru: дай, дай мне (сокращение от give me)
type: informal — a verb fused with its object pronoun
register: informal — normal in speech, blunt on paper
contrast: Only *me* fuses this way: there is no ✗ *gimme him* or ✗ *gimme you*. *Gimme* has also hardened into set expressions — *gimme a break* is disbelief, not a request for rest, and in sports talk *a gimme* is a noun meaning something so easy it is granted without being played. Written out, *give me* is always correct.

senses.gloss: The reduced *give me*.
examples: *Gimme* a call when you land.
*Gimme* that wrench — I can reach it from here.
*Gimme* a second, I'm almost done.

ru: дай мне, дай-ка (сокращение от let me)
type: informal — a verb fused with its object pronoun
register: informal — normal in speech, out of place in edited writing
contrast: Only *let me* reduces this way; *let him* and *let her* do not. *Let us* has its own contraction, *let's*, and that one is fully standard writing. *Lemme* is always followed by a bare verb: *lemme know*, *lemme see*, *lemme think*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *let me*.
examples: *Lemme* know what time you're getting in.
*Lemme* see that picture again.
*Lemme* think about it overnight.

ru: не знаю (сокращение от (I) don't know)
expands: *don't know*, usually with the *I* swallowed into it
type: informal — a whole clause reduced to two syllables
register: informal — speech and text messages only
contrast: *Dunno* normally stands for the entire sentence *I don't know*: the subject is gone, not merely reduced. It does not conjugate, so ✗ *he dunno* is not the pattern in General American — for a third person say *he doesn't know*. In writing it reads as a shrug, which is sometimes exactly wrong in an email.

senses.gloss: The reduced *(I) don't know*.
examples: *Dunno* — ask Marcy, she was there.
I *dunno* if the store is still open.
I *dunno* what he wants me to say.

ru: вроде, как бы, довольно (сокращение от kind of)
type: informal — a preposition swallowed into the noun before it
register: informal — texts and casual writing, not essays or business email
contrast: The library also lists *kinda* as an adverb of degree, and that softening use is the commoner one: *kinda tired*, *I kinda like him*. The literal *kind of* reduces the same way after a noun or a question word: *what kinda car is that?* In edited writing, use *kind of*, *somewhat* or *a little*. Its twin is *sorta*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *kind of*, both as a hedge and in its literal sense.
examples: I'm *kinda* tired — can we do this tomorrow?
That's *kinda* what I was afraid of.
What *kinda* car did she end up buying?

ru: вроде, отчасти (сокращение от sort of)
type: informal — a preposition swallowed into the noun before it
register: informal — texts and casual writing only
contrast: *Sorta* and *kinda* are interchangeable as hedges, with *kinda* the commoner of the two in American speech. Neither belongs in edited prose — write *sort of*, *somewhat*, or drop the hedge altogether.

senses.gloss: The reduced *sort of*.
examples: It *sorta* works, but not the way we planned.
I *sorta* promised I'd be there.
She's *sorta* my boss and *sorta* not.

ru: из, вон из (сокращение от out of)
type: informal — a two-word preposition run together
register: informal — speech, dialogue and lyrics
contrast: *Outta* is *out of*, not *ought to* — that one is spelled *oughta* and is a different word. It lives mostly in fixed phrases: *get outta here*, *outta luck*, *outta nowhere*, *outta my way*. Written *out of* is always available and always safe.

senses.gloss: The reduced *out of*.
examples: Get *outta* here before he sees you.
We're *outta* milk again.
That came *outta* nowhere.

ru: много (сокращение от lot of в обороте a lot of)
type: informal — a quantifier phrase run together
register: informal — speech and casual writing
contrast: *Lotta* carries only the *lot of* part, so the article in front stays: *a lotta people*, not ✗ *lotta people*. The plural *lots of* reduces the same way, to *lotsa*. Both are speech spellings; *a lot of* is the written form, and *alot* is never a word.

senses.gloss: The reduced *lot of* inside *a lot of*.
examples: There were a *lotta* people at the funeral.
That's a *lotta* money for a used car.
He's got a *lotta* nerve showing up here.

ru: надо, должен (сокращение от have to)
type: informal — the obligation *have to* run together
register: informal — the spelling is casual, the pronunciation is universal
contrast: Listen for the /f/: the obligation *have to* is pronounced with a voiceless /f/ and /t/, which is why it is spelled *hafta* and not ✗ *havta*. The possessive *have* keeps its /v/ — *I hafta go* but *I have a car*. The third person reduces the same way, to *hasta*. Compare *gotta*, which delivers the same obligation through *have got to*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *have to* of obligation.
examples: I *hafta* be up at five tomorrow.
Do you *hafta* leave so early?
You don't *hafta* answer that.

ru: мог бы (сокращение от could have)
type: informal — a modal plus a reduced *have*
register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use *could have* or *could've*
contrast: *Coulda* is what *could've* actually sounds like, and it is the source of the commonest spelling mistake in American English: ✗ *could of*. There is no *of* in it — the *-a* is a reduced *have*, which is why the participle follows (*coulda gone*, *coulda known*). The set *woulda, coulda, shoulda* is a fixed phrase for pointless hindsight.

senses.gloss: The reduced *could have* before a past participle.
examples: I *coulda* told you that a week ago.
We *coulda* been there by now if we'd left on time.
You *coulda* gotten hurt doing that.

ru: сделал бы (сокращение от would have)
type: informal — a modal plus a reduced *have*
register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use *would have* or *would've*
contrast: Same trap as *coulda*: the *-a* is *have*, never *of*, so ✗ *would of* is always an error. *Woulda* belongs to the unreal past — it needs a condition somewhere, stated or understood: *I woulda called* implies *if I could have*. Written out it is *would have* or *would've*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *would have* before a past participle.
examples: I *woulda* called, but my phone was dead.
She *woulda* said something if she'd known.
That *woulda* been a lot easier.

ru: надо было, следовало (сокращение от should have)
type: informal — a modal plus a reduced *have*
register: informal — speech and dialogue; in writing use *should have* or *should've*
contrast: The *-a* is *have*, so ✗ *should of* is an error here too. *Shoulda* is almost always regret about something that did not happen: *I shoulda known* means I did not know and wish I had. Regret about someone else's behavior comes out as blame — *You shoulda called*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *should have* before a past participle.
examples: I *shoulda* known better than to trust him.
You *shoulda* seen his face.
We *shoulda* booked the earlier flight.

ru: потому что (сокращение от because)
type: informal — a conjunction with its first syllable gone
register: informal — dialogue, lyrics and texts; write *because* in anything edited
contrast: The apostrophe stands for the missing *be-*, so the careful spelling is *'cause*. The same word is also written *cuz*, and both are equally informal. Do not confuse it with the noun *cause* (a reason, a purpose), which rhymes with *laws* and is a different word entirely: *the cause of the fire* has nothing to do with *'cause it was cold*.

senses.gloss: The reduced *because*.
examples: I left early *'cause* I had a headache.
We're not going, *'cause* the roads are bad.
Just *'cause* he said it doesn't make it true.

ru: потому что (разговорное написание because)
type: informal — a conjunction with its first syllable gone
register: informal — texting and lyrics above all
ambiguity: *Cuz* also writes the clipped *cousin* — *my cuz* is a relative, not a reason, and in some circles it is a friendly term of address. What follows tells you which: the conjunction takes a whole clause, the noun takes nothing.
contrast: *Cuz*, *'cause* and the British *cos* are three spellings of one reduced *because*. *Cuz* is the texting spelling; *'cause* keeps the apostrophe that marks the missing syllable and looks slightly more careful on the page. Neither belongs in school or business writing, where the full *because* is the only option.

senses.gloss: The reduced *because*, spelled as it sounds.
examples: I'm staying in *cuz* it's freezing out.
He quit *cuz* they wouldn't give him weekends off.
Not *cuz* I want to — *cuz* I have to.

ru: вы, вы все (сокращение от you all; южное и афроамер.)
type: dialect — the second-person plural that standard English lacks
register: regional — Southern and African American English, and now widely used far beyond them
contrast: The apostrophe replaces the missing letters of *you*, so the spelling is *y'all*, never ✗ *ya'll*. English lost its plural *you* when *thou* died, and *y'all* is the most successful of the forms that fill the hole, beside *you guys* (national), *youse* (northeastern) and *you'uns* or *yinz* (Pittsburgh). *All y'all* is not redundant: it forces the reading 'every single one of you'. The possessive is *y'all's*. The library also lists *y'all* as a personal pronoun, where its associative use — *Is y'all coming Sunday?* said to one person but meaning her whole household — is treated in full.

senses.gloss: The contracted *you all*, used as a plural *you*.
examples: *Y'all* want to grab something to eat after?
I'll see *y'all* at the game on Saturday.
All *y'all* need to be on the bus by seven.

ru: ты, вы (редуцированное you)
type: informal — the weak form of a pronoun, not a dialect form
register: informal — the spelling is casual, though the sound is what everyone produces
contrast: *Ya* is nothing but unstressed *you* written down: not Southern, not plural, not uneducated. After a /t/ or /d/ it stops being a separate syllable at all and fuses with the word before it — *got you* becomes *gotcha*, *did you* becomes *didja*, *what are you* becomes *whatcha*, *bet you* becomes *betcha*. It is never a possessive; the reduced *your* is *yer*. The library also lists *ya* among the personal pronouns.

senses.gloss: The reduced *you*, subject or object alike.
examples: See *ya* Monday — I'll leave the keys at the desk.
I'll call *ya* as soon as I land.
*Ya* never know, it might clear up by noon.

ru: их, им (редуцированное them)
type: informal — a reduced object pronoun, leaning on the verb before it
register: informal — in writing only; in speech it is simply the normal unstressed form
contrast: The surprise is that *'em* is not a clipping of *them* at all. It descends from Middle English *hem*, the native plural object pronoun that the Norse-borrowed *them* pushed out of the written language while the old form survived in the mouth. The apostrophe writes down a history nobody remembers. Fixed phrases keep it: *give 'em hell*, *knock 'em dead*, *round 'em up*, *you can't win 'em all*. When the pronoun carries stress it is always *them*. The library also lists *'em* among the personal pronouns.

senses.gloss: The unstressed *them*, written as it sounds.
examples: Just tell *'em* we'll be ten minutes late.
I saw *'em* leaving as I pulled in.
Round *'em* up and load *'em* on the truck.

ru: час, часов (о времени по часам; из of the clock)
type: fixed — frozen from *of the clock*, the last survivor of a whole family
register: standard — fully standard everywhere, in speech and in the most formal writing
contrast: The apostrophe does exactly what it does in *can't*: it marks something missing, here the whole of *of the*. Nothing else survives of the old pattern — *five of the clock* has been gone for two centuries. Use it only with whole hours from one to twelve: *at six o'clock*, but *at 6:30* and never ✗ *6:30 o'clock*. Never combine it with *a.m.* or *p.m.* (✗ *seven o'clock p.m.*); say *seven p.m.* or *seven o'clock in the evening*. Russian *в шесть часов* is *at six o'clock* or simply *at six*. The library also lists *o'clock* as an adverb of time.

senses.gloss: The contracted *of the clock*, used after a number to name a whole hour.
examples: The store opens at nine *o'clock*.
It's almost three *o'clock* — we should get going.
I'll meet you at the station at six *o'clock*.

ru: мэм, мадам (вежливое обращение; сокращение от madam)
type: fixed — frozen from *madam*
register: standard — polite address, near-obligatory in the South and in the military
contrast: The apostrophe replaces the *-d-* of *madam*, so the spelling is *ma'am*, not ✗ *mam* or ✗ *maam*. Its counterpart is *sir*, which is not a contraction of anything. *Yes, ma'am* is plain courtesy in the South, in the armed forces and in service work; in the Northeast and on the West Coast it can land badly on a younger woman, who may hear it as a comment on her age. The unreduced *madam* now survives only in titles like *Madam President* and in the salutation *Dear Madam*.

senses.gloss: The contracted *madam*, used to address a woman politely.
examples: Yes, *ma'am*, I'll have that ready by Friday.
Excuse me, *ma'am* — you dropped your scarf.
Can I get you anything else, *ma'am*?

ru: полагаю, наверное (сокращение от suppose)
type: informal — a verb with its first syllable gone
register: informal — dialogue and casual speech; write *suppose* otherwise
contrast: *S'pose* loses the whole first syllable of *suppose*. It turns up in two places above all: the lukewarm agreement *I s'pose so*, and *s'posed to*, which is how *supposed to* actually sounds — note that the *-d* goes silent too. Do not mix *s'posed to* up with *hafta* and *gotta*: *supposed to* reports a rule or expectation somebody else set, and often hints that it was broken.

senses.gloss: The reduced *suppose*, including the *supposed to* of expectation.
examples: I *s'pose* so, if there's no other way.
You're not *s'posed* to park there.
What am I *s'posed* to tell her?

ru: что ты…? (сокращение от what are you или what do you)
type: informal — a question word fused with its auxiliary and pronoun
register: informal — speech, dialogue and lyrics only
ambiguity: The same *whatcha* hides two different auxiliaries. Before an *-ing* form it is *what are you*: *Whatcha doing?* Before a bare verb it is *what do you*: *Whatcha want?* Nothing in the spelling tells you which — only the verb that follows.
question: *Whatcha* exists only in questions; there is no statement form. The full versions are *What are you…?* and *What do you…?*, and the *ya* inside it is the reduced *you* fusing with the /t/ before it.

senses.gloss: Standing for *what are you*, before an *-ing* form.
examples: *Whatcha* doing this weekend?
*Whatcha* looking at?
*Whatcha* laughing about?

senses.gloss: Standing for *what do you*, before a bare verb.
examples: *Whatcha* want on your burger?
*Whatcha* think of the new place?

ru: спорим, точно (сокращение от bet you)
type: informal — a verb fused with a reduced *you*
register: informal — speech and dialogue
contrast: *Betcha* is *bet you* with the /t/ and the /j/ of *ya* fused into a /tʃ/ — the same change that turns *got you* into *gotcha* and *what are you* into *whatcha*. Two patterns account for nearly all its uses: *I betcha* introduces a prediction, and *You betcha* is a fixed interjection meaning an emphatic yes, associated with the Upper Midwest and with nobody's actual wager.

senses.gloss: The reduced *bet you*, in predictions and in the fixed *You betcha*.
examples: I *betcha* he shows up twenty minutes late.
You *betcha* I'll be there.
*Betcha* can't guess who I ran into today.
